shows.title: Tide of Returns
shows.artist: Repatriates Collective (Verena Melgarejo Weinandt, Khadija von Zinnenburg Carroll, and collaborators)
shows.description:
Tide of Returns takes on one of the thorniest live issues in museum politics — the repatriation of looted and displaced cultural objects — and stages it as an immersive, sensory installation rather than an argument. The centerpiece, From My Mother's Country, floods the nave of the former Church of San Lorenzo with sand carried in part from the Gulf of Carpentaria in Australia and thousands of shell-and-fabric figures modeled on Dadikwakwa-kwa, sacred dolls recently returned to the Warnindilyakwa people by Manchester Museum. Video and sound documenting the objects' remaking and their journey back to community hands run through the installation, turning restitution into something felt in the body rather than just read about.

Alongside it, Verena Melgarejo Weinandt's Weaving Connections uses three-channel video of braiding, washing, and preparing textiles to think through how German cultural institutions have historically fabricated and displayed Indigenous identity — and what it costs to unwind that. Blue-toned threads and black braids recur through the piece as a visual rhyme for water's own capacity to connect and cleanse.

Curated by Khadija von Zinnenburg Carroll as part of her long-running Repatriates research project, the exhibition draws on real, recent cases — Namibia's restitution from Berlin, Australia's from Manchester — without illustrating them literally. It's a fitting subject for Ocean Space, whose whole program treats water as a connective and reparative force, and one of the more quietly urgent shows to see during this Biennale year.

shows.title: Darkness Visible: The Long Shadow of Dictatorship
shows.artist: Nicanor Aráoz, Eduardo Basualdo, Marcelo Brodsky, Luis Camnitzer, Flavia Da Rin, Sergio De Loof, León Ferrari, Ana Gallardo, Eduardo Gil, Guillermo Kuitca, Liliana Maresca & Marcos López, Gianni Mestichelli, Marta Minujín, Luis Pazos, Néstor Perlongher, Aldo Sessa, Archivo de la Memoria Trans, La Organización Negra
shows.description:
This group exhibition, organized by Buenos Aires's Museo de Arte Moderno in partnership with Spazio Punch, marks the 50th anniversary of the 1976 coup that installed Argentina's last military dictatorship. Nineteen artists and collectives are brought together across generations and media — from 1970s conceptual and political works through recent photography, video, sculpture and archival material — tracing how Argentine artists responded to state terror, censorship, torture and forced disappearance, and how those wounds still surface in the present, including in ongoing violence against women.

The checklist reads like a cross-section of postwar Argentine art history: Guillermo Kuitca and Marta Minujín alongside León Ferrari's incendiary text-based works, Marcelo Brodsky's photo-based memory projects, and the archival testimony of Archivo de la Memoria Trans, which documents a community doubly erased by dictatorship-era repression. Curators Victoria Noorthoorn and Patricio Orellana of the Museo Moderno, working with Spazio Punch's Augusto Maurandi, frame the museum and, here, the project space itself as a civic platform — a place where art functions as historical testimony and human-rights advocacy rather than simple aesthetic object.

The show's title nods to Milton's description of hell in Paradise Lost, using the oxymoron to describe art's capacity to illuminate what dictatorship tried to keep hidden. It's a heavy, historically dense exhibition, but an unusually rare chance in Venice to see a museum-scale survey of Argentine political art, staged fittingly in a former brewery turned artist-run space on Giudecca.

shows.title: Las Invisibles (Guatemala Pavilion, 61st Venice Biennale)
shows.artist: ARKEO, Luana Bottallo, Jorge Chavarría, Manuel Navichoc, Ana Lorena Núñez, SOY artistic group, Elsie Wunderlich
shows.description:
Las Invisibles is Guatemala's Biennale pavilion, and it puts Mayan women at its center — not as subjects to be depicted but as the source of the show's whole method. Corn, stone, clay, and the domestic hearth recur as materials and motifs, standing in for the repetitive, physically demanding labor (grinding maize on a hot comal, tending a household) that sustains community life while literally wearing away the body, down to erasing fingerprints.

Curators Elsie Wunderlich and Stefania Pieralice built the exhibition around this idea of quiet, unrecorded endurance — the show's title translates as "The Invisible Women" — and the participating artists, working across sculpture, textile, and installation, treat ancestral Mayan knowledge and ritual as a living practice rather than an ethnographic subject. The result is less a survey of Guatemalan contemporary art than a focused meditation on gendered labor and cultural memory.

Staged in Spazio Berlendis' cavernous former shipyard, the installation has room to breathe, and the venue's raw industrial materials — brick, timber, water access — sit well against a show so concerned with earth, hearth, and handmade objects.

shows.title: The Poetics of Correspondence (Grenada Pavilion, 61st Venice Biennale)
shows.artist: Edward Bowen, Arthur Daniel, Josine Dupont, Alexandra Kordas, Lilo Nido and Chris Mast, Jeverson Ramirez, The Holzwege Group, Russell Watson
shows.description:
Grenada's national pavilion takes correspondence — letters, currents, cultural exchange across water — as both subject and method, using it to think through the island's history of creolization and diaspora. The eight participating artists work across installation, time-based media, and archival-style interventions, building a show that favors accumulation and layering over a single unifying image, in keeping with its interest in networks rather than fixed positions.

Curator Daniele Radini Tedeschi frames the pavilion as an exercise in listening to quieter registers of relation — intimacy, resistance, and exchange conducted at a human scale rather than through grand historical narrative. Given Grenada's small size and the outsized way Caribbean pavilions have punched above their weight at recent Biennales, this is a good opportunity to see how a small nation stakes out curatorial ground amid the sprawl of national pavilions across the city.

Housed in Spazio Berlendis' restored shipyard, with its water access and soaring ceiling height, the installation gets a raw, light-filled setting rather than a white cube — a good match for a project so concerned with tides, currents, and the passage of things across water.

shows.title: Lee Ufan
shows.description:
Dia Art Foundation's Venice presentation of Lee Ufan is a rare chance to see seven decades of the artist's work laid out across eight galleries in a single building. Lee, a founding figure of Japan's Mono-ha movement and a key voice in Korean Dansaekhwa painting, has spent his career testing how little a painterly gesture or a placed stone needs to say to change the feeling of a room. The show moves from historical paintings to new canvases and large installations, including a site-specific commission made for the Procuratie space, and traces how his vocabulary of restraint and repetition has stayed consistent even as its scale has grown.

Curated by Dia's director Jessica Morgan, the exhibition treats the Procuratie's sequence of rooms as an extension of Lee's own thinking about space — each gallery is staged to slow the visitor down rather than accumulate incident, in keeping with his long-standing interest in the charged emptiness between objects. The presentation coincides with Lee's ninetieth birthday and runs alongside a parallel show of his work at Dia Beacon in New York, making this the most substantial European survey of his work in some time.

For anyone who knows Lee mainly through single iron-and-stone Relatum pieces in museum collections, seeing this many works together — paintings, sculpture, and a new commission — clarifies just how patient and cumulative his project has been.

shows.title: Alighiero Boetti
shows.description:
This survey of Alighiero Boetti gathers roughly a hundred works across eight galleries, tracing the Turin-born Arte Povera artist's career from the late 1960s to his death in 1994. It opens with early self-portraiture and the doubled identity he formalized in 1972 by signing his work "Alighiero e Boetti," then moves through the bodies of work he is best known for: the embroidered Mappe, in which world maps are rendered as colored flags stitched by Afghan artisans; the obsessively dotted Biro drawings; and the permutational Aerei, in which fleets of airplanes are arranged according to shifting systematic rules.

What makes the show worth the visit is how clearly it lays out Boetti's central trick — handing off execution to other hands (embroiderers, assistants, chance procedures) while keeping tight authorial control over the conceptual framework. Curator Elena Geuna organizes the rooms so that this tension between control and delegation, order and disorder, builds cumulatively rather than being stated once and repeated.

Boetti has had major retrospectives at MoMA, Tate, and the Reina Sofía, but a show of this depth in Venice — a city that hosted his work at the Biennale itself in 1990 and again in 2001 — gives the material a different kind of resonance, especially the Mappe, which are as much about networks of collaboration and geography as about painting.

shows.title: Sharing Legacy
shows.description:
Sharing Legacy pairs the late feminist sculptor Nancy Azara with her longtime partner Darla Bjork, a painter and practicing psychiatrist, in a show built around forty years of shared life rather than shared style. Azara's carved and gilded wood sculptures, drawn from matriarchal archetypes and the recurring image of the tree as body and ancestor, sit alongside Bjork's encaustic paintings and drawings, which mine the layered, half-hidden textures of the psyche. Both artists trained through the New York Feminist Art Institute, and that grounding shows in the show's insistence on gesture and material as forms of testimony.

What holds the two practices together is less subject matter than temperament: an expressionist handling of surface, a comfort with roughness and accretion, and an interest in what sits beneath the visible layer of a work. Seeing Azara's totemic, weathered forms next to Bjork's warm, waxy fields makes a quiet case for collaboration as a kind of portraiture — two people's decades together rendered obliquely through their separate tools.

Curated by Jen Dragon and Fanny Perez, the exhibition is a fitting late tribute to Azara, whose sculpture helped define a generation of feminist art practice in New York, and a chance to see her work in dialogue rather than isolation.

shows.title: Future Light
shows.description:
Future Light brings Gabriella Kirby back to the Veneto village her grandparents left after the Second World War, and the homecoming gives the show its emotional charge. Working across canvas, paper, and plaster, Kirby builds mixed-media compositions that move between plant, animal, and human form, looking for the protective and communicative structures — skins, membranes, roots — that let fragile things survive.

The paintings favor organic, gestural abstraction over illustration: trembling edges, layered plaster, and forms that read as both wound and shelter. Vulnerability and memory are the explicit themes, but the more interesting undercurrent is inheritance — how trauma and resilience travel across generations and continents, surfacing here in materials that themselves feel weathered and built-up over time.

Arriving in Venice during the 61st Biennale, two generations and seventy-five years after her family's emigration, Kirby treats the return less as nostalgia than as a way of testing what persists. It's a small, personal show, but one whose questions about belonging and renewal reach well past the artist's own family history.

shows.title: Yields of Fray
shows.description:
Leo Frontini's *Yields of Fray* is the Los Angeles-based painter's first European solo exhibition, timed to the 61st Venice Biennale and organized by the curatorial platform Private Waters with the Boateng Family Art Foundation. The show gathers eight paintings, two works on paper, and three marble sculptures made in 2025 and 2026, all pulled from a single body of work in which the artist stages scenes suspended between waking life and invented, parallel realities.

Frontini treats canvas, paper, and stone as three dialects of the same language: recurring figures migrate between a painted vision, a pencil study, and a carved form, so that a single dreamlike image can be read across media within the same room. The work draws on memory and the subconscious, letting tender and unsettling registers sit side by side — a strategy closer to symbolist narrative painting than to straightforward figuration, with the marble pieces grounding the more hallucinatory paintings in physical weight.

It's a compact but ambitious show for an artist still early in his career, arriving in Venice on the strength of two well-received gallery exhibitions in New York and Los Angeles. Seeing the sculptures and paintings together, in the intimate rooms of SPARC* just off Campo Santo Stefano, gives a clearer sense of how Frontini's imagery moves between mediums than any single-medium presentation could.

venue.name: SPARC* - Spazio Arte Contemporanea (Galleria d'Arte Santo Stefano)

shows.title: The Promise of Change
shows.description:
Michael Armitage paints on Lubugo bark cloth, a material beaten from fig trees in Uganda whose seams, holes, and stitched patches are visible right through his pigment. That rough, living support is central to why his paintings feel so charged: a scene of a political rally, a nightclub, or a body pulled from a river doesn't sit on a neutral ground, it fights its way through one. This survey at Palazzo Grassi, the artist's largest to date, brings together forty-five paintings alongside more than a hundred works on paper, tracing how he moves between reportage and reverie.

Armitage, who was born in Nairobi in 1984 and splits his time between Kenya and the UK, draws his imagery from a wide net: news photographs of the violently contested 2017 Kenyan election, the lockdowns of 2020-21, East African folklore, colonial-era painting, and touchstones of Western art history from Goya to Gauguin. The effect is layered and sometimes deliberately hard to parse, with multiple vantage points and timelines compressed into a single canvas. A gallery devoted to his drawings and studies gives a rare look at how these dense compositions get built up in stages.

What makes the show worth crossing Venice for is the way Armitage refuses to let horror and beauty cancel each other out. Migrants crossing water, riot police, and mythic hybrid figures are rendered in the same lush, acid-bright palette, so that the paintings seduce before they unsettle. It's a strong, ambitious use of the Palazzo Grassi's two floors, and a good test case for what history painting can still do in the present tense.

shows.title: Third Person
shows.description:
Lorna Simpson made her name in the 1980s pairing staged photographs of Black women's bodies with fragmented text, taking apart how images claim to tell the truth about identity. This exhibition at Punta della Dogana, organized with the Metropolitan Museum of Art, skips past that early photographic work almost entirely to concentrate on the paintings, collages, and sculpture she has made since the mid-2010s, when she started working in oil, ink, and silkscreen at a much larger scale.

The show is built around three loose bodies of work. One gathers dense, crowded compositions with echoes of protest and unrest, populated by fractured figures. Another is a suite of Arctic and ice-field paintings, cool blue-grey landscapes derived from old expedition photographs that Simpson treats less as travelogue than as a metaphor for erasure and instability. A third, staged inside Tadao Ando's concrete cube at the heart of the building, is given over to monumental images of women whose faces and bodies resist easy reading. A forty-panel collage installation, built from decades of clipped and archived source imagery, functions almost like a study room for her whole practice, showing how she stockpiles and recombines found pictures before they become paintings.

At over fifty works, this is described as the largest European presentation of Simpson's art in more than a decade, and the first to give this much room to her turn toward painting. Seeing it inside Punta della Dogana's raw brick-and-timber galleries, with the lagoon light coming through Ando's windows, adds an extra layer to paintings already obsessed with atmosphere, memory, and things half-dissolved.

shows.title: Peggy Guggenheim in London: The Making of a Collector
shows.description:
Before there was a palazzo on the Grand Canal, there was a single room in Mayfair. This exhibition, the first large-scale museum show devoted to it, reconstructs Guggenheim Jeune, the gallery Peggy Guggenheim ran in London for eighteen months between January 1938 and June 1939, and argues that everything she later became as a collector was worked out there first.

The gallery's brief, restless program gets rebuilt here through roughly a hundred works and a trove of archival material: Kandinsky's first solo show in London, a Cocteau exhibition, an early UK collage survey, and a sculpture show that scandalized the press. Paintings by Kandinsky, Mondrian, Sophie Taeuber-Arp, Wolfgang Paalen, Rita Kernn-Larsen, Barbara Hepworth, and Henry Moore stand in for what actually hung on those walls, alongside photographs, letters, and gallery ephemera documenting the friendships, with Marcel Duchamp among them, that steered Guggenheim's eye toward abstraction and Surrealism.

It's a smart, research-driven complement to the permanent collection one floor away: instead of just marveling at the finished Venice museum, you get to watch its taste get formed in real time, through gambles and failures as much as triumphs. The show travels next to the Royal Academy and the Guggenheim in New York, but seeing it in the city where Peggy eventually settled, a short walk from the works she went on to buy, gives it a particular charge.
